sections.html:
Maryland sets a few mandatory lease items, and some clauses can't be enforced at all. Under Real Property § 8-208, a landlord offering five or more dwelling units must use a written lease. Without one, the tenancy is presumed to run for one year from first occupancy unless the tenant ends it with one month's written notice.

Every lease must include:

  • A statement about the habitability of the premises, or the condition the parties agreed on
  • Each party's duties for heat, gas, electricity, water and repairs
  • A receipt for the security deposit
  • A copy of the current Maryland Tenants' Bill of Rights from the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs in the Department of Housing and Community Development

A landlord must also hand a prospective applicant the proposed lease on written request, with no signature or deposit required.

sections.h2: Lease clauses a landlord can't enforce
sections.html:
Section 8-208 lists terms that are unenforceable. A tenant can recover actual damages and attorney's fees if a landlord includes or tries to use one. Prohibited terms include:

  • Confession of judgment, or a waiver of the tenant's legal remedies or a jury trial
  • A shorter notice-to-quit period than the law requires
  • A right to take the premises or the tenant's belongings without termination and formal legal process, unless the property is abandoned
  • A penalty on a tenant for calling law enforcement or emergency services
  • A waiver of the tenant's right of first refusal under § 8-119

Late fees are capped at 5% of the rent due for the period. On weekly leases the cap is $3 per week or $12 per month. An automatic renewal clause longer than a month must be set apart with room for the tenant's written acknowledgment, or the landlord can't enforce it.

The landlord must give a receipt, keep the money in a proper account, and offer a move-out inspection. The receipt has to tell the tenant about the right to a move-in inspection and the right to be present at the move-out inspection. It also has to warn that noncompliance can mean a penalty of up to three times the deposit withheld plus attorney's fees. Without a receipt the landlord owes the tenant $25, and copies must be kept for two years.

Deposit ruleMaryland requirement
Where it is heldInsured institutions with in-state branches, in interest-bearing accounts used only for deposits
When it is depositedWithin 30 days of receipt
Tenant's request to attend inspectionCertified mail at least 15 days before moving, with move date and new address
Timing of inspectionWithin five days before or after the move date
InterestSimple interest, no less than 1.5% a year, only on deposits of $50 or more, and none unless held six months

A landlord who skips the inspection steps forfeits the right to withhold money for damages.

sections.h2: What happens to the deposit when a landlord sells
sections.html:
The seller stays liable for the deposit unless the full amount and an accounting go to the buyer. Under § 8-203, the original landlord remains responsible for the deposit plus interest until it is transferred with an accounting to the transferee. Any successor in interest is liable for failing to return it.

A new landlord must accept a tenant's surety bond and can't demand an extra deposit during the current term. Creditors of either party can't attach the deposit.

If you're planning a sale, reconcile the deposit records before closing. That transfer and accounting is what moves the liability off you. In a cash sale with a short timeline, pull the ledger and the tenant's receipt early so the numbers are ready when the buyer's side asks for them.

sections.h2: Do tenants get a right of first refusal when the owner sells?
sections.html:
In many cases, yes. Section 8-119 gives tenants of one to three unit residential rentals a right of first refusal. The tenant must have lived there six months or more and be named on the written lease.

  • Owner plans a public listing: Send notice before listing. The tenant has 30 days to make a written offer, and the owner has five days to accept or counter.
  • Owner gets an unsolicited third-party offer: Send notice at that price. The tenant has 30 days to match before the owner can accept.
  • Third-party offer at least 10% below the lowest price offered to the tenant: Notice and a new 30 day window
  • Tenant declines early: Owner may list

Many transfers are exempt, including sales to family members, foreclosure and tax sales, estate and trust administration, transfers by will or inheritance, and properties of four or more units. A violation carries a fine of up to $1,000, and liability stays with the owner rather than the property after closing. Owners send copies of notices to the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs through its website.

For a lease term longer than a month, the landlord must give at least 90 days written notice before a rent increase. Section 8-209 sets shorter periods for shorter terms: 60 days for a term over one week up to one month, and 7 days for a week or less under a written lease (21 days if there is no written lease).

Notice goes by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, or electronically if the tenant elected that. A landlord can't make electronic notice a condition of the lease application. Local laws may require longer notice. Whoever holds the landlord's position when the increase is sent is bound by these rules, so a new owner who plans to raise rent after closing should count the days from the date notice actually goes out.

It begins with a written notice and a 10 day cure period, then a District Court case. Under § 8-401, the notice must state the intent to sue for possession, and the complaint must give the date the notice was delivered.

  • Trial is set for the fifth day after filing.
  • If the court finds rent due, possession is ordered within 4 days after trial. A physician's certificate can extend that up to 15 days.
  • A warrant of restitution can issue after 7 days. The landlord must order it within 60 days of the judgment or the possession judgment is stricken.
  • Warrants are stayed during extreme weather and must be executed within 5 days after conditions end.
  • Either side may appeal to circuit court within 4 days.

A tenant can redeem by paying all past-due amounts, court costs and fees before the eviction is carried out, unless the tenant has three rent-related possession judgments in the prior 12 months.

sections.h2: Eviction for breaking another lease term
sections.html:
For a lease with a stated term that allows repossession on breach, § 8-402.1 requires 30 days written notice, or 14 days where the behavior shows clear and imminent danger of serious harm. The landlord then files a written complaint in District Court.

The court must find the breach substantial before it orders eviction. Either party may appeal to circuit court within 10 days. Accepting a payment after the notice doesn't waive the breach notice or the possession judgment unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

A tenant can use rent escrow only for serious, dangerous defects such as no heat, light or running water, inadequate sewage disposal, or serious structural or fire hazards. Under § 8-211, cosmetic problems, small cracks and a lack of air conditioning are presumed not to qualify, and the tenant must first notify the landlord. A wait of more than 30 days after notice is presumed unreasonable.

Section 8-208.1 bars retaliation for good-faith complaints, joining a lawsuit, taking part in a tenants' organization, or calling police or emergency services. A tenant who wins can recover damages up to three months' rent plus fees. An action taken more than six months after a protected act isn't treated as retaliatory.

faqs.q: Does a Maryland landlord have to use a written lease?
faqs.a: Yes if the landlord offers five or more dwelling units. Without a written lease the tenancy is presumed to last one year from first occupancy.

faqs.q: How much can a Maryland landlord charge as a late fee?
faqs.a: No more than 5% of the rent due for the period. For weekly installments the limit is $3 a week or $12 a month.

faqs.q: What notice is needed for a rent increase?
faqs.a: For a term longer than one month, at least 90 days written notice. Shorter terms have 60 or 7 day notice periods, and local laws can add more.

faqs.q: Do tenants get first chance to buy a rental house in Maryland?
faqs.a: Often. One to three unit rentals fall under the right of first refusal in § 8-119 for tenants who have lived there six months and are on the lease, with a 30 day window and many exemptions.

faqs.q: Who is liable for the security deposit after a sale?
faqs.a: The original landlord stays liable unless the full deposit and an accounting are transferred to the new owner. Any successor in interest is also liable for failing to return it.
